TESTIMONY OF A LOUISIANA COLORED MAN—
WHIPPED AND SHOT AS IN THE DAYS OF SLAVERY
—THE EXODUS NOT AT AN END.
[BY TELEGRAPH TO THE TRIBUNE.]

WASHINGTON, Aug. 29.—J. E. Bruce, a colored man and Editor of The Exodus, of this city, a paper which circulates chiefly among the colored people, has received a private letter from a correspondent in Louisiana, giving something of the political outlook from a colored man's point of view. The writer says:

The prospect of the colored race getting along in Louisiana is glorious. In April, a crowd of white roughs went to a colored church in East Baton Rouge, drove away its occupants, closed the church and whipped some of the members. On several plantations in the State several colored laborers organized and demanded wages at a rate that they could live on. The Governor sent the militia to the places where the strike occurred, arrested the men and placed them in prison on trumped-up affidavits.

The exodus still continues from Louisiana, Texas, Alabama and Mississippi. Every St. Louis packet that leaves this port always carries several persons who are fleeing the wrath of Democratic rule. The Negro in the South.
SHINGTON, Sept. 1.—J. E. B.
The Negro in the South.
WASHINGTON, Sept. 1.—J. E. Bruce, a colored man and editor of The Exodus, of this city, a paper which circulates chiefly among the colored people, has received a private letter from a corrospondent in Louisiana, giving something of the political outlook from a colored man's point of view. The writer says:

The prospect of the colored race getting along in Louisiana is gloomy. In April, a crowd of white roughs went to a colored church in East Baton Rouge, drove away its occupants, closed the church and whipped some of the members. On several plantations in the state several colored laborers organized and demanded wages at a rate that they could live on. The Governor sent the militia to the places where the strike occurred, arrested the men and placed them in prison on trumped-up affidavits.

The exodus still continues from Louisiana, Texas, Alabama and Mississippi. Every St. Louis packet that leaves this port always carries several persons who are fleeing the wrath of Democratic rule. I learn that several hundred are expected soon to emigrate from Caddo, Bossier and adjoining parishes of Louisiana; also from Augustine and other counties of Texas to the north and west.

The colored Republicans of this state have held no meeting as yet to indorse Garfield and Arthur. Several ward clubs have on their own responsibility indorsed our Republican nominee.

In Jackson Parish of this state the white people whip the colored people just as they did in the days of slavery. In Caddo a white man unmercifully beat an intelligent colored lady because she would not be his concubine. In Falls county, Texas, the colored people are determined to go to Liberia, and have called for aid from the American colonization society. So you can judge from this outline what Democratic rule is doing south, and what the result will be if they succeed in getting the presidential chair.

During the beginning of July a colored man was shot in the court-house in the presence of judges, sheriffs and lawyers, because he had married a white woman, the sister of the would-be murderer. Again, on July 4, 1880, a colored man was killed by three white villains because he was walking with what they took for a white woman, when she was his own sister. The Colonization Council is holding regular sessions, and considering the whole matter relative to our race leaving here.

Red Devils Demoralized.

WASHINGTON, Sept. 1.—The following telegram has been received at the war department from Brigadier General Ord, under date of San Antonia, Texas, August 27:

Grierson by telegraph from Ruitman, dated yesterday reports as follows: My scouts have returned after closely following the Indian trail to the Candeleria mountains, Mexico, and report the Indians in a badly crippled and demoralized condition, having their wounded with them and their stock played out. He also reports that the Mexican troops have neither attacked the Indians nor got in their way, and have evidently given them a passage toward the west, only skirmishing with small parties who were stealing stock from the Mexican cattle men. The Indians crossed the road leading from El Paso to Chihuahua only a few hours after Col. Valle with a small detachment passed south to ward that place, and they have gone via the Santa Maria river in the direction of Dequesman. This information is confirmed by a telegram from the commanding officer at Fort Bliss, who states that the Indians were there in camp with their wounded from the 28th of July, upon their first crossing the river to Texas, until the 12th of August, when Victoria with the last of his force was the second time driven back into Mexico. The loss of the Indians in the fights at Rattlesnake canon and in the several skirmishes and other fights was certainly not less than thirty killed and wounded, very probably over forty, and without fresh horses add rest to reecuperate, they are not now in a condition to act in a body against any organized force, as they are now in Mexico at least 150 miles to the westward of Fort Quit man.

no wonder they doubt whether there ever was a Fifteenth Amendment passed or not. "In East Baton Rouge, a crowd of whites went to a colored church, drove away the occupants, whipped the members and closed the church." "In Caddo, white men unmercifully beat colored women who chose to remain virtuous." "A colored man is shot for walking with his own sister, because she is supposed to be a white woman." In every State where labor is needed to build railways or State roads, negro convicts are worked as slaves in everything but name, half-starved and treated with a brutality which the slave-owner never exercised, from motives of policy. The traveller still sees the great gangs of blacks at work with the overseer at watch, whip and gun in hand. They turn on him the same stolid look of hopeless misery.

It is all so like the old time that the middle-aged man fondly fancies the last twenty years have been a dream. He is still young. There was no war, no emancipation; the South never had its arrogance, its folly, its brutality beaten out of it by a savage punishment. Surely the old familiar faces are not all gone. Foote, of Mississippi, is still hopping up and down in Congress; Brooks is belaboring Summer; Toombs, and Jefferson Davis, and Marcy still sit in our high places; the crack of the slave-driver's whip is heard daily in the Senate, and Northern mudsills keep their places.

If the old times have come back with such pathetic familiarity merely at the prospect of renewed Southern ascendance, what may we expect if the South should really gain control of the White House?—[N. Y. Tribune.

The Southern method of securing that great boon, "a pure ballot," for which the Democratic platform pronounces in its second article, have been resumed in Texas, Mississippi and South Carolina.

In Texas, Amos T. Bissell, a Union sailor, and now a revenue officer, made a temperate Republican speech to the negroes. But he complained that while ample provisions were made for the education of white children, only partial provision was made for colored; and that assessment for taxes was two or three times as much on the property of colored people as on the same kind of property belonging to white people; and, further, that while colored people confined in jail awaiting trial, were hired out for the benefit of the county treasury, white men in the same fix were not interfered with. He advised the colored people to strive to elevate and improve their condition. For this offence he was threatened with death by three distinct parties, and that with such details as terrified the man into giving up his situation under the Government, and flying to Galveston for safety. His enemies had the insolence to apply to the Galveston collector to secure his removal for the offence of making Republican speeches. We are glad to see that Attorney General Devens has taken the matter up, and orders an investigation. He is reported as saying that "If the courts of the National Government cannot protect the right of freedom of speech there will be no such tolerated in the South." But we greatly doubt the power of the United States Courts, as at present constructed, to secure that or any other right to the Southern Republicans. This is what could not be said of the courts of any other civilized nation.

In Mississippi, the brother of the murdered Col. Dixon visited Yazoo to attend the deathbed and funeral of the Colonel's widow, who has died of a broken heart. Mr. Dixon had the audacity to talk politics, and to predict the election of Garfield and Arthur. He was warned to leave Yazoo, and was told they would have no such talk there, nor any voting for Garfield.

event-1880-07.A2:
South Carolina Bull-Dozers Under Orders.
CHARLESTON, S. C., July 24.—The first bingle-blast in the campaign to assemble the Republicans of Barnwell county at Blackville, on July 27, for the purpose of ratifying the nominations made at Chicago, has aroused the Democratic bull-dozen to action, and the kind of reception they will accord the Republicans can be conjectured from expressions in the Barnwell newspapers. The People says: "We learn that E. W. M. Mackey and W. N. Taft, the bravest and most brazen Radicals in the State, together with numerous lesser party lights, will be in Blackville on Tuesday. There is one lesson which the Republicans of this State have not yet learned. The sooner they know and become reconciled to the inevitable, the better it will be for them. It is this: The Democrats have obtained control of the State of South Carolina, and they intend to retain it at every hazard and in spite of the utmost efforts of local enemies and their Northern allies. We are requested by the highest competent Democratic authority to invite all Democratic candidates to attend the Republican meeting. They are expected to be on hand. The Barnwell Sentinel, after cutting the object of the meeting, says: "It is the duty of the Democratic party to have representatives at this meeting from all parts of the county. So let all clubs send fair representatives among them. Let them be men who will nail lies to the wall as fast as they are told. Democratic capsid candidates should attend to a man.

The clubs mentioned are the notorious Red Shirt, Rifle and Sabre Clubs which committed the outrage and murder in 1876 in Ellerton, only a few miles from Blackville, in the same county. They will, of course, attend the meeting, and, in accordance with their usual method, become masters of ceremony, invite Democratic speakers on the stand, and order the Republicans to step off, and if the latter do not choose to listen to the former they can go away. The result will be a Democratic "pow-wow." It would be an excellent opportunity for Northern Republicans to come to the meeting, unknown and unannounced, and witness the treat Republicans receive in this State who are brave enough to assert their manhood. South Carolina Bull-Dozing.
From the Phila. Press..

Please allow me space enough in your widely circulated paper to give your readers and the public generally a faint sketch of the unlawful treatment the colored Republicans are now undergoing in this county since the grand Garfield and Arthur ratification meeting, which took place here on the 27th of July. The Democrats tried in every way possible to prevent the colored people from attending the meeting; but they would not be persuaded, and so we we had quite an enthusiastic meeting, between five and six thousand colored between five and si
to order out a sufficient number of men to work on and repair the different public roads for three days, work to commence on the 28th of July. Now, when when the County Commissioners, or sub-Commissioners, Warners found out there was to be a Republican ratification meeting meeting on the 27th of July they changed the order from the 28th to the 26th. (By which one one of these so-called officer's authority it was changed / officer's authority it was changed / am unable to say ) But, however, it was changed, and about twenty-five out of four or five hundred were notified of the change. The others, who never knew of any change taking place, prepared to begin taking place, prepared to begin the work on the 28th instant. No notice of any change appeared in either of the county Democratic papers. And now now they are arresting them from $10 to $15 or putting them them in jail from fifteen to thirty days. They have have extorted out of these poor people already from two to three hundred dollars. Besides this, many have to remain in prison, leaving their wives and little suffering children at home. And God only knows how many are laying out in the woods and swamps to prevent being arrested. And again, after the majority of these poor men returned home, they, the next morning (the 28th). went to the several places of appointment to work the roads and the sub-Commissioners objected to their working, and on returning home to their families many were discharged and driven from off the farms on which they were working. (Many of these people were also working for shares of the crop.) Other colored men who are farming on their own land were visited by a band of these armed midnight riders, and they cursed and abused and threatened and also warned them never to attend another Garfield Republican meeting.

And now, Mr. Editor, I wish you had been among us on Monday or Tuesday to see the colored ministers traveling across the country trying to raise money enough to release their church brethren from imprisonment. I could write you hundreds of pages, for every hour in the day I am receiving divers complaints from different sections and from the officers of the different Garfield and Arthur Clubs in the county of the unlawful treatment they are receiving on account of their politics. But as I only asked for a small space I will close by saying that through all the treatment they have or may receive they are determined to cast their votes for Garfield and Arthur.

Very respectfully yours,

FREDERICK NIX, JR.,
Co Chair'n of the Republican Party of Barnwell Co.

Blackville, S. C., Aug 11, '80.

The Boston Herald, independent, calls Senator Conkling's late speech in New York "the speech of a partisan rather than a patriot—of an adversary rather than a statesman." "It is not such a speech as we were accustomed to hear from Daniel Webster, nor as the people flocked to hear from Henry Clay; but Mr. Conkling belongs to the new school of politicians—the men who 'boss' instead of lead; who dominate by the force of their personality and will, rather than by their intellect or the power of their ideas. A forceful speech is this New York effort, but, judged by any high standard, it cannot be called an eloquent or great one. Its logic is the logic of events—its figures those of the arithmetic. This process may make a strong speech, but it does not produce oratory. Its appeals are to prejudice. Even its pretense is offensive. It is marred by sneers and sarcasms, and, while these may please enthusiastic admirers, they were never known to persuade men into the speaker's way of thinking. So great, indeed, is Senator Conkling's characteristic failing in this direction, that he could apparently hardly wait to get through with his stilted exordium before dropping the gall of his venom upon President Hayes. We are surprised that this passage was not hissed. It would have been if delivered by anybody but the 'imperious' Senator, in the 'imperial' city of New York."

The Herald continues:

Coming to the issues of the campaign, Senator Conkling really presents but one, though he gives to it many turns and twists. And this issue is, whether the Democratic party deserves to be intrusted with uncontrolled power in the nation. Speaking to this question, nothing is more natural than that he should consider its record for the past dozen or twenty years, and this of course he finds no difficulty in painting very dark, for the Democrats themselves, by their series of what we have denominated blunders that are worse than crimes, and crimes that are worse than blunders, have furnished him plenty of dark material. When, however, he accepts the Southern or sectional phase of this issue, with mock regret, wishing it were not so, but saying that it is—and that in twelve states "there is no free debate, no equal rights"—he knows that he is not telling the truth. Before the great meeting at Blackville, S. C., early in the summer, the Republican organs were very sure that no such gatherings would be permitted, and the impossibility of free discussions was urged as a reason for abandoning a canvass of the South.— When, however, it transpired that the meeting was not disturbed, they changed their tune, and said a canvass would not amount to anything, as there would be cheating in the count. The canvass of the South was deliberately abandoned, in order that that the managers might treat "the solid South" as so much funded capital for use at the North, and not, as Senator Conkling declares, because free debate was impossible. The power of the South in the Democratic party and the danger to the settlements of the war constitute the burden of his speech. But has not the South the right to vote as it pleases—provided, always, that it does so freely and fairly? Or does the Senator propose that "the Southern question" shall be kept alive until the South joins a party which has abandoned its organization in most of their States, or until the Democratic party will agree to die and be buried? When is this indictment, bad as we concede it to be, to run out? Will the North and West probably pay any less proportion of the taxes for the next dozen years? Under what conditions will he agree that the Republican party is no longer essential to the preservation of the government, and is the heaven-ordained ruler of the country? The whole argument of his speech would make the dynasty perpetual.

huntsville-huntsville-1880-08.A2:
UNBLUSHING FRAUDS.
How the Bourbon Majority was Manufactured—Republican Votes Thrown Aside or Counted for the Democrats—Facts and Figures Proving the Shameful Work.
Democrats — Facts and Figures Proving the Shameful Work.

WASHINGTON, Aug. 11.—Senator Morgan, of Alabama, makes the remarkable assertion that the recent election in his State was as fair as any election ever held anywhere, and that no election could be more fair. Private letters are received every day here which tell the true story. One gentleman, in a letter to Hon. Commissioner Raum, describes the scene at the polls in Huntsville. Processions of voters who intended to vote the Democratic ticket came to the polls led by brass hands and were not molested, of course; but when the colored men came forward in procession, shouting for the candidates of the combination ticket, they were attacked and dispersed some of them being badly hurt.

He continues:

"An election law in this State which forbids the numbering of tickets to corp respond with the tally-list, and in this way destroys every evidence that tends to establishing a basis for parging the polls from illegal votes, together with the fact that the Democratic managers took pains to put on as one of the Judges of Elections at each place men of Republican antecedents, who could not read in many instances, certainly establishes a margin for fraud that it appears cannot be detected and punished.

The evils complained of by the Republicans were treated with indifference, and the Democrats refused to make any correction.

The State has, perhaps, given a larger Democratic vote than ever before since she has had a Republican vote, and under the Election laws and the means resorted to with Democratic machinery, it is not any surprise to any man that is at all informed upon Alabama or Southern politics."

One of the leading men of the State sends the following to Secretary Sherman: "The late election in this State, as most of us anticipated, was a mere farce. Whatever of decency remained in the Democratic party was on this occasion entirely cast aside, and frauds the most unblushing and stupendous committed. In many counties, where the population was largely colored, the Republicans did not vote, knowing that their votes would swell the Democratic majority. In some counties where we had a county ticket in the field we brought out the full Republican strength, and it was in such cases the counting-out was done. In Lowndes county, Judge M. Duffield got 3,380 votes actually voted for him and put into the box, each voter showing his ticket openly as he went to the polls.

The Democratic vote of the county is not over 1,300, and yet they returned a majority of 1,360 against him. In two beats there was an honest count. He carried one by over 400 majority, and the other, which was always carried by the Democrats, he carried by 4 majority. In Scott's beat, Perry County, where tally was kept in like manner, the Republicans openly voted over 500 votes and the Democrats 40, and this beat returned a Democratic majority of 230. These are only 'specimen bricks. When you apply it to the State you can see how the Democrats got their 75,000 majority." The writer then inserts the following from a private letter sent to him from Montgomery. 'Such a grand rally of the Republicans of the county has not been seen since 1868. Such intelligent determination to carry the election on the part of the colored people was never known before. But votes don't count. The election was the biggest fraud you ever saw or heard of. The Democrats themselves admit it. We know it. It is perfectly useless to make any effort in this State from present appearances.

The real fact is, in this State the Democrats intend to hold the State Government at all prices and hazards and this they regard as their imperative duty. Of course they say if we win in the national campaign it will be so much the better, but they looked upon Alabama as their country, and the United States and the power of the National Government as a foreign power and a despotism put upon them against their will and consent." He closes his letter to the Secretary as follows: "This is the true key to the Southern problem. Home rule and State rights mean that no man elected by the votes of black men shall be permitted to hold office in a Southern State. They consider it a high moral duty to defraud the black man of his vote."

WASHINGTON, D. C., Aug. 11.—To-day Gen. Raum, Commissioner of Internal Revenue, received a letter from an Alabama Republican, who was in Huntsville on election day. The writer says:

"I was in Huntsville on the day of the election. The polling-places were opened at 7 o'clock, according to law. Shortly after the polls were opened I heard a brass band strike up a lively tune, and, looking out of the window, saw a number of colored men in line marching to the polls, headed by the band, and under the control of friends of the Democrats. After this came a similar number of colored voters, who intended voting for the Republican combination ticket, shouting for Harrison, the Republican candidate for Probate Judge, and, when fairly up to the voting-place, an attack was made on them by a young white man and Democrat named Tom Sprogins, who, encouraged by the mob spirit of his friends, succeeded in dispersing for a time the friends of Harrison. In the meantime knocking down with a cane and severely wounding one colored man, and striking several others. This unprovoked attack had the desired effect of intimidating some of the men thus intending to vote. After they were disposed in this manner it is unknown how they voted, unless the large Democratic majority at Huntsville tends to explain the matter."

The writer continues at considerable length, giving other instances of violence and intimidation, and showing the true inwardness of the so-called election.

HOW ALABAMA WAS CARRIED.
THE DEMOCRATIC VICTORY DESCRIBED BY ONE WHO SPEAKS FROM KNOWLEDGE-ALTERATIONS AND FRAUD. [BY TELEGRAPH TO THE TRIBUNE.]
SPEAKS FROM KNOWLEDGE—ALTERATIONS AND FRAUD.

[BY TELEGRAPH TO THE TRIBUNE.]

WASHINGTON, Aug. 23.—A letter has been forwarded from Huntsville, Ala., to Commissioner Raum for publication. It is from Mr. Hewlitt, a deputy marshal, a native of Alabama, and a man of recognized standing. The substance of his story, as related by the letter, is as follows:

As a basis of my complaint, I charge:

First—That the election machinery is all in the hands of the Democratic party, and under the workings of that machinery the margin for fraud is beyond any question.

Second—That the vote of Madison County, or rather the count, exceeded by over six hundred that taken at any election that has been held since 1876.

Third—That the votes as cast at Triana and Whitesburg are known to me to have been falsely counted, and the Democratic ticket returned as elected, contrary to the wishes of a majority of the voters.

Fourth—That there was an assault made upon the line of Independent voters at the Huntsville box, which intimidated and hindered a fair election.

In regard to the first charge I would say that when it became necessary to select the inspectors, the persons selected by the Republicans and Independents were generally rejected, and in many cases ignorant colored men arbitrarily selected to represent the party.

Concerning the second charge, I allege that the vote (or the count) is larger than at any election since 1876. In the year 1876, when party spirit ran high, the aggregate vote in the county was 6,200, while in the late election the aggregate vote was 6,838, any excessive vote of over 600. In the Democratic primaries, with the combined influence of all of the candidates and their friends, only about 2,600 voters were drawn out, and at the regular election only a short time subsequent, the Democratic candidate for Probate Judge received 3,876 votes.

To the third charge I desire to invite particular attention, as that involves the inspectors at Triana and Whitesburg. At the Triana Prescinct the Republicans have been in the habit of carrying it by majorities ranging from 200 to 250, and at Whitesburg 75 and upward. At the late election the Democratic ticket was returned as elected at Triana by 174, and at Whitesburg by 71. The candidates for Probate Judge were selected as the basis for the calculation. I was at Triana on the day of election. The officers of the colored clubs sent me to meet them about one-half mile distant from the polls, with the tickets they desired to vote. This I did, and went with them and saw them deposit the same with the inspector. After the result was anounced there was such a conviction of fraud on the part of voters that the presidents of the clubs called their voters together, and obtained affidavits from them in the effect that they voted for Harrison for Judge.
nounced there was such a conviction of fraud on the part of voters that the presidents of the clubs called their voters together, and obtained affidavits from them to the effect that they voted for Harrison for Judge. These affidavits have been sent in, and are now held as evidence, giving Harrison, at Triana, a vote of 373 instead of 217. I put upon a number of tickets voted three different names for Coroner, as follows: "A. F. Murray," 10 votes; "J. T. Green," 6 votes; and "L. A. Wortham," 10 votes; but when the returns were declared no reference was made to the above votes for Coroner, indicating that they may have been displaced and Democratic ballots substituted for them.

In relation to the fifth charge I state what is known to at least one hundred voters. There was an assault made by Democrats upon a number of Independent Republican voters at Huntsville on the day of election which had a tendency to demoralize and intimidate them. In this affair one colored man was knocked down and others were assaulted with sticks and pistols. This is in conflict with what The Huntsville Independent has to say about the election in its issue of the 5th inst. It says: "Peace prevailed in Madison last Monday. We have always taken the position that temperate language is best in all things. We therefore simply say that if any man, whether correspondent, editor, or what not, says there was any buldozen here, he lies! Yes, he lies!" Then, as if to seal the "victory" won at the election, about 150 Democrats left Huntsville for the purpose of visiting Madison, Triana and Whitesburg, carrying with them the "little Democrat" (a small cannon) and a lot of whiskey. The Independent of the 5th inst. says: "Never anything like it. There was never anything like the rejoicing in the good old County of Madison. Some twenty vehicles and 150 Democrats, white and colored, left here yesterday for Madison, Triana and Whitesburg with the 'little Democrat,' and they will have a grand time." I respectfully submit that if the manner in which the election has been carried on at Huntsville, Triana and Whitesburg is a fair sample of the balance of the State, the majority of 90,000 Democratic votes is no longer a mystery, but may be truthfully called the monumental fraud of the age.
huntsville-huntsville-1880-08.A7:
WADE HAMPTON CORNERED. The dispatches from Staunton, Va., published in 'THE TRINXE this morning are interesting reading. Gen. Wade Hampton made a speech to his Virginia brethren, and, never dreaming of the presence of newspaper reporters in that remote region, talked right out in meeting, and with the unreserved freedom usual among Southern men when upon their own sacred soil. It seems that one Gordon was employed to send a report of the speech of Hampton to the New York World. There being another meeting in Staunton on the same day, which he was to report for some other paper, he made an arrangement by which, in consideration of the editor of the Virgintan furnishing him with a report of the second meeting, he agreed to furnish that paper with a report of the Hampton meeting. This was carried out, but when his report was furnished the words in controversy were discovered to
he missing, Gordon declaring that he would not send them North to be misconstrued; but the Virginia insisted on their insertion and they were printed. The whole testimony in the case is conclusive as to the general correctness of the language attributed to Hampton in his appeal to the Virginians to be united and true to the principles for which the War had been fought, and for which the patriots, Lee and Jackson, had contended.

Mr. Yost, the editor of the Virginia, certainly vindicates his integrity, his fairness, his manliness, and his ability, and the Senator is unquestionably in a most embarrassing and painful position. Had the Democrats permitted his speech to stand as he delivered it, and as he undoubtedly intended to be understood, Senator Hampton would have been saved a world of trouble. As it is, he stands convicted of having used the language attributed to him and of the weakness of trying to screen the Democratic party from responsibility at the North for the honest sentiments he so frankly expressed in the Valley of Virginia to an audience nearly all Democrats.

In the meantime the correspondence proves that the letter published by the Washington Post purporting to be written by Senator Hampton turns out to be a forgery, and is so declared by Hampton himself.

The editor of the New York World is also convicted of garbling and mutilating the speech of Hampton, and also of striking out of the report of the speech of Senator Vance, at the same meeting, that portion in which he urged the Virginians to repudiate their State debt and instate the glorious example of noble old North Carolina.

Senator Hampton, from under the cloud which shadows his attempt to make Virginians believe that voting for Hancock was but contending for the same principles for which Stonewall Jackson died and Leo fought, dexterously undertakes to give a wholly new version to his opinions on the subject. He says now that by the War the right of "peaceable secession" was determined forever, but he does not say that the doctrine of State-sovereignty and independence of National control has been settled. He now lamely, after being detected in his Staunton speech of appealing to Virginians to vote as Lee and Jackson would vote if they were alive, says that the Democratic party has nothing to do with the doctrine of peaceable secession. His attempt at this late day to patch up his Staunton speech, addressed to Virginians, by a postscript intended for the Northern eye, adds to the evidence of his tergiversation and of his moral weakness. A manly adherence to his Staunton speech would have been far more honorable than his present humiliating and equivocating denial of his real sentiments. His attempt, after conviction, to make a new speech for the North, will deceive no one, and will not extricate either him or his party from the fate that awaits them at the National ballot-box.

THE MONUMENTAL FRAUD OF THE AGE.

The story of the Democratic frauds in Alabama cannot be told too often. It is the only State in the South which has yet held an election bearing upon the general result in November, and it has set a fashion, for the last time it is to be hoped, that will be followed in the other Southern States, in pursuance of their desperate conspiracy to seize the Government and once more assert "the principles for which Lee and Stonewall Jackson fought." Every day brings fresh testimony as to the outrageous frauds perpetrated in that election, and shows that they were not confined to Lowndes and Montgomery Counties, but were practiced all over the State. Where the Bourbons feared to use fraud they resorted to bulldozing and absolute violence, and where it would not do to drive Republicans or Greenbackers away from the polls by force, they took possession of the ballot-boxes and stuffed them with Democratic votes. The resources of infamy were ample and varied enough to suit all localities. Thus, with bulldozing on the one hand and ballot-box stuffing on the other, every law of elections was openly and unblushingly violated, and the election itself was a supreme and unmultigated farce. Not a man on the Bourbon ticket, which flaunts its majority of 60,000, was legally elected.

The Greenbackers appear to have been the principal victims of these outrages, since the Republicans, knowing there would not be a fair count, did not as a rule attempt to vote. A letter from Huntsville to the Indianapolis Sun, a Greenback organ, confirms what has already been stated in Republican papers as to the general frauds committed, but is of special interest as it concerns those committed in a portion of the State not previously heard from. Early in the morning, the Bourbons, with a brass band at their head, and armed with sticks and pistols, paraded through the streets, and when the polls were opened took possession in a threatening manner and voted their men, compelling all others to stay away. During the forenoon several colored men who came up to vote the Greenback ticket were assaulted and driven off with clubs, and pistols were drawn by the score. Previous to the election the Republican and Greenback candidates were threatened with violence if they continued in the field, and several of them, to save their lives, withdrew from the canvass,—among them Judge Craig, Circuit Judge in Dallas County, who was renominated, and was not only threatened by anonymous letters, but was warned by the Selma Times, a Bourbon paper, that his candidacy would cause trouble and be dangerous to him.

A. H. Byrd, a well-known gentleman in Green County, Alabama, has had the courage to publish a letter in the midst of the Bourbons, in which he says:

As they would not allow us a manager or clerk at the polls in Forkland, I got two high-toned gentlemen, both Democrats, to assist me in keeping a tally-sheet outside of the polls. We did this in the interest of justice and fair play, but failed most significantly. Those who voted the Fusion ticket came forward, voluntarily exhibited both sides of the same to show that there were no marks or figures on it, folded it up again, and then, while we closely watched them, marched forward and placed it in the hands of one of the managers. When the polls were closed our tally-sheet showed a total vote of 718, which exactly corresponded with that kept by the managers. We saw 619 out of the above-stated number go into the hands of the managers, and are willing to swear that they were all Fusion tickets except one, and yet when they counted the vote they only gave us 313. I can call together almost any day at least 600 voters in Forkland that who will come forward and swear to the above facts, and be glad of the opportunity to do so. Green County has immortalized herself with dishonor.

In confirmation of these charges is the letter which was printed in The Timone of yesterday, from Mr. Howlitt, a Deputy Marshal and native Alabamian, living at Huntsville, to Commissioner Raum. John H. Harris, a colored democratic speaker from Virginia, attempted to make a speech at New Castle on Saturday night, and was stoned and forced to seek the protection of the Sheriff.
john-h-harris-newcastle-1880-07-31.A7:
The report started in Wilmington that the Philadelphia, Wilmington & Baltimore Railroad Company were about to lease the Eastern Shore railroad, running from Delmar to Crisfield, seems to be unfounded.

Georgetown is becoming noted for fast horses. Horace Adams has made the latest addition. He calls him "Dreadful" and swears that the nag has a record between two and three minutes. This horse belonged to ex-Senator Bayard, who paid $1500 for him.

DEATH OF ISAAC J. JENKINS.—Isaac J. Jenkins, formerly a well-known Delawarean, died at his residence at Asbury Park, N. J., on Friday last at the age of 61 years. Mr. Jenkins was a native of Sussex county. He was a Republican and held several offices under the Federal and State Governmen, being at one time Deputy Collector of the port of Wilmington. He leaves a wife and five children.

CAMP MEETING CASUALTY.—A gentleman, near Kenton, on Sunday night week, at the camp ground, while in the act of handling his child to his wife, who was seated in the carriage, let it fall upon the ground, when he picked it up he did not perceive any trouble but when they arrived home, the child was found to be dead. The Dr. in attendance said its neck was broken by the fall. It was about five months old.—Delawareon.

Steps have been taken to build another hotel at Rehoboth Beach. A meeting of Baltimore and Wilmington men was held there last week, at which it was decided that subscription books should be opened in Baltimore and Wilmington, and a committee appointed to solicit subscriptions, several hundred dollars being subscribed by those present at the meeting. It is intended to have the new house ready for use next season.

There was a rough-and-tumble row in the Lincoln Republican Club room at Wilmington on Wednesday night. The city executive committee was in session at the time. Tom Saville and Jim Hawkins settled an old feud, which was stirred up by a question of politics, and banged away at at each other like two pugilists. At one time a general row seemed imminent, but the corbatants were seperated and order was finally restored. As a result Hawkins has lost his place as letter carrier.

The new editor of the *Daily News*, in the midst of the stirring incidents of the day, exhausts nearly a column in making an analytical description of a tick. The tick of course crawled into his office and must have made a wonderful impression on him. for he tells us that the Northerners who don't receive them by mail regard them as large as bull-frogs. It is needless to say that when he had given two or three turns on it with his No. 11 brogan, there wasn't much left of that tick.

CAMDEN CAMP.—This camp after a two weeks meeting closed yesterday. As a social gathering for the people of Kent county, it was a delightful resort, separated from harmful influences with enough of grace for seasoning, and better in every way than the seaside resort with their irregularities. There was considerable difference of opinion as to the time of closing, a number being in favor of going home on Friday and it was decided in the board of *Managers* to hold over to Tuesday only by a majority of one. Lev. A. W. Lightbourne who had had change of it up to that time declined to longer remain in the management, and its control passed to the direction of Rev. J. Robinson. The supply of ministerial help was much less than usual, owing, it is said, to the invitation being general rather than special.

Appoquimunk, with Sam Townsend engineering them, says the "Downtown Mile," are getting spunky, and are going to have things in New Castle county fixed. They declare that this thing of "a few tricksters at the county meetings at New Castle trying to cheat the Democracy of the county out of nominating candidates for Sheriff, Coroner, Legislators and Levy Countmen by ballot," is played out. They call for a S te convention to make a new constitution, in which it shall be set forth that all officers shall be nominated by ballot and elected by the people by ballot, and that after said constitution is so made by the convention it shall be left to the people to ratify or reject. This sounds Democratic. The war horse is getting his war paint on, and going to make more trouble in the ranks.

A Democratic Negro.—A colored man calling himself John H. Harris claiming to hail from Virginia has been creating a sensation in Harford county, Md., and at Wilmington. The Bel Air Argyle declares him an undoubted swindler. His object was to get up Hancock and English clubs among the colored people and had some encouragement from the Gascie and others, his contributions from different Democratic officials amounting to $25 or $30. He was an annomaly in political circles. The Republicans don't want him, of course, and it is decidedly repugnant to the inborn spirit of Delaware Democracy to have its ideas expounded by a colored man. The Democratic party of Delaware is pre-emently a white man's party, and the "nigger need apply rue," adopted some time ago, still represents the sentiments of the majority. Therefore the colored "orator" was snubbed, by the Jefferson Club. The only way they could use him would be to cause a dissatisfaction with those who vote the Republican ticket. THE ATTACK UPON THE VIRGINIA NEGRO HARRIS AT NEW CASTLE, DEL.—NO EULOGIES OF THE DEMOCRATIC PARTY DESIRED BY NORTHERN NEGROES.
THE ATTACK UPON THE VIRGINIA NEGRO HARRIS AT NEW CASTLE, DEL.—NO EULOGIES OF THE DEMOCRATIC PARTY DESIRED BY NORTHERN NEGROES.

[Wilmington (Del.) Every Evening.]

Harris found the court-house at New Castle closed upon his arrival, and a crowd of 300 or 400 persons, mostly blacks, gathered upon the pavement and street in front of the building. After a futile search for the janitor of the building, in which he was assisted by two or three white persons, Harris returned, and mounting a carriage from which the horse had been detached and stabled, he proceeded to make an open-air speech. As he went on to eulogize the Democratic party, and to show the colored portion of his audience why they should vote that ticket, some of the latter grew restless, mutterings were heard, and it was evident that a storm was brewing.

The speaker continued, however, unmindful of those indications, to harangue his audience for nearly half an hour. At this time he was saying something like the following:

“Suppose the colored people had to look entirely to the Republican party for their living, what kind of a living would they get? But they get their living principally from the Democrats, and if they want a favor done, if they want legal advice, they go to a Democrat. If you can trust the Democrats as your legal advisers, why cannot you trust them as your political advisers? I tell you that the southern people are your best friends—”

Just here a stone weighing about a pound came hurling through the air, but missing the orator it struck a white man named McNulty, who was standing near the carriage, inflicting a severe wound upon his head. McNulty was picked up by his friends and taken to Ferris & Son’s drug-
rage, inflicting a severe wound upon his head. McNulty was picked up by his friends and taken to Ferris & Son's drugstore, where he received the necessary surgical attention.

A scene of some confusion followed. Several small stones came flying after the large one and unpleasantly near the heads of some of the bystanders, while the sheriff proceeded to summon a posse comitatus in anticipation of a serious row.

Meanwhile Harris continued his speech about in this style, while the terrified driver, with pale features and bristling hair, besought and implored him to get down out of the vehicle and conceal himself. "For my part," said Harris, "I have thrown off the painted mask of Radicalism, and claim to be a freeman, and I do not propose that any political party shall drive me as a sheep to the polls." He was going on to talk about the policy of the negroes dividing and not voting the Republican ticket quite so unanimously, when the growing disturbance caused him to withdraw.

During his temporary absence the frightened driver hitched up his horse and drove hurriedly off, seeing, or imagining he saw, a line of colored men armed with bricks fringing both sides of the street nearly to the edge of town.

Finding his conveyance gone, Harris started to walk home, followed by a large crowd of his own color and a few whites. Upon reaching Orange street he was persuaded to return and place himself under the protection of the sheriff, who kept him in the jail building until morning, and then sent him to Wilmington. After the stone-throwing, which was supposed to have been done by negroes, a party of white men made a rush in the direction from whence they came, and the assailants would have been speedily arrested could they have been found.
Harris declares his firm intention of speaking here to-morrow night, according to programme, and says he was prevented by sickness from speaking at Bel Air. He spoke this morning of threats having been made by some of his own color to mob the house in which he puts up to-night, declaring that they "won't suffer any Democrat nigger to make a speech here or stay in the town."
john-h-harris-newcastle-1880-07-31.A10:
Criminal.
James T. De Jarnette has been indicted for the murder of his sister, whom he found in a house of ill-fame, at Danville, Va. He attempted suicide in jail, Saturday.

John W. Clements Shaw, one of young Kalloch's witnesses, who swore that Chas. DeYoung fired the first shot, has been convicted of perjury in San Francisco.

A dispatch from Tuscarora, Nevada, says: Deputy Sheriff W. B. Weaver and William B. Hammond fought over a game of cards, when Hammond was killed and Weaver mortally wounded.

John H. Harris, colored, democratic speaker from Virginia, attempted to make a speech at Newcastle, Del., on Saturday night, but was stoned and forced to seek protection of the sheriff.

Max Burckhardt, editor and proprietor of the Humorist, a German weekly in San Francisco, committed suicide Sunday by taking morphine. Cause unknown. He was a native of Berlin and 50 years of age.

John F. Erpenbeck, aged 35, saloon keeper of Baltimore, committed suicide Saturday afternoon on his wife's grave in Holy Cross cemetery by shooting himself in the head with a pistol. His wife died two months ago.

George Montigriffo, 65 years old, of New York, was robbed of $1800 on board one of the Stonington boats, Friday, night. He went to sleep on a bench on deck, and the money, the savings of a lifetime, was taken from his pocket.

Pietro Balboa, the condemned Italian wife murderer in New York, was notified, Tuesday morning, of the governor's refusal to interfere with the death sentence. He exhibited but little emotion, remarking that he would exhibit no cowardice at the last. Preparations for the execution on Friday commenced at the Tombs that afternoon.

A Nashville dispatch reports the shooting, at Woodland Mills, six miles from Union City, of Harry Crenshaw by Alex. Ellison, colored. Crenshaw went to quiet a boisterous crowd of colored people, fired into it, and Ellison returned the fire from a double-barreled shot-gun, with fatal effect. Ellison was arrested. Lynching is expected.

The gun case of Bodine, a member of the American rifle team, who had just returned from the international contest at Wimbledon, on examination by the custom officers at New York, on Monday, was found to contain two pairs of kid gloves, six pairs of ladies' silk hose, six ladies silk scarfs, and three, rolls of black silk, 134 yards in all. The goods and the case of rifles were seized under the Smuggling act and sent to the seizure room.

Josiah Carr, who murdered his nephew, Caleb Carr, at Coventry, R. I., last week, committed suicide in Kent county jail Tuesday night in a very ingenious manner. He placed a handkerchief about his neck and putting a stick through the fold, tightened it as one would a tourniquet until strangulation ensued. His trial was to have been begun in a few days. Carr shot his nephew while the two were engaged in a hot quarrel.

Edward Egan, from Dubuque, Ia., a bar-keeper at Malta, a small town three miles from Leadville, was killed Monday by a ranchman named James Brady, an old settler. Brady was returning from a circus and, while under the influence of liquor, entered the saloon where Egan was bar-keeper, the latter being asleep on the counter. He was helping himself to drink, when Egan awoke. A few blows were exchanged, when Brady drew a revolver and shot Egan through the heart. The murderer escaped, but was subsequently arrested.
john-h-harris-newcastle-1880-07-31.A11:
Our Delaware Bulldozers.
Gur Delaware Bulldozers.

A colored man named Harris came to this city last week and announced his intention to attempt to organize a colored Hancock and English Club. The JOURNAL has kept well posted concerning his movements and does not care to conceal the fact that it has not the highest respect for the man, because his habits and associations are not such as to inspire respect while ugly stories come from the scene of his previous operations. Nevertheless we cheerfully announced his meetings, having no desire to refuse the man a hearing, and we paid slight attention to the threats we heard that he would be mobbed if he undertook to make a speech.

It appears, however, that the threats were not mere idle talk, and that Harris, having attempted to make a speech in favor of the Democratic candidates, at New Castle last Saturday evening, was mobbed by a crowd of negroes, and some one in the crowd threw a brick at him, which severely wounded a white man who was among the listeners. Now, Harris' good or bad character has nothing to do with this phase of the subject. He is certainly as good as some white men who make political speeches, let him be as
ntemperate or worthless as he may.
He had a perfect right to make
a political speech if he wanted to, and to
make it on which side he preferred. Yet,
for attempting to make it, he is assaulted
by a mob of negroes and the people who
are horrified about alleged outrages on
free speech way down South, in some
community about which they know nothing,
are entirely calm over this deliberate
attempt at bulldozing a negro right at our
very doors.

Here is a new and striking illustration
of the insincerity of the pretended regard
for the negro for his own sake. According
to the stalwart theory the war was
chiefly fought that men of Harris' color
might enjoy freedom of speech and the
right to express, by tongue and ballot, their
political convictions; yet we doubt
if there is a Republican in this
community really grieved at heart
because this fellow's right
to free speech has been lawlessly abridged.
The right the war was chiefly fought to
establish in the opinion of these philan-
throphists was the right of negroes to
make Republican speeches and vote the
Republican ticket, and there is absolute
indifference to the rights, privileges or welfare of any of the race who manifest a disposition to vote the Democratic ticket or urge others to do so. If this is the temper negroes display in Delaware where they never have had any power, what reason is there for doubting the truth of the stories about the wholesale persecution they resort to in South Carolina to prevent members of their own race from voting the Democratic ticket there?

We have no doubt that there is just as much intimidation of negroes by negroes in the South as there is of negroes by white men. It cannot be possible that men who own little properties, as thousands of negroes in South Carolina and the other Southern States do, or that even steady laborers who want peace and order in the community and schools for their children, can desire the restoration of the sort of governments which taxed real estate out of the hands of its owners, mortgaged the credit of the States beyond hope of redemption, almost, and even stole the school fund which was the hope of the race that gave the thieves power. We do not think so meanly of the negro race as to believe that the better members of it would want to restore such government as that ; and yet we hear on quite as good authority as any bloody-shirt story ever had, that these men are threatened with violence if they vote the Democratic ticket, and that negro preachers and negro women are the most addicted to stirring up the wrath of the mobs.
john-h-harris-newcastle-1880-07-31.A16: SAVAGE BRUTALITY—FREE SPEECH AND FREE BALLOT DENounced BY REPUBLICANS OF PENNSYLVANIA.—It appears that the negro man Harris, who was in this State some weeks ago, claiming the right to speak as a Democrat to the negro citizens of New Castle and Wilmington, and was stoned at the former place and mobbed at the latter by the Republicans, went to Chester. What he had been doing there we do not know. But a despatch says he was to deliver an address on Tuesday evening, when he was met by other negroes and knocked down and kicked in the face, and badly beaten. This is the much vaunted "free speech and equality" the citizens of Pennsylvania extend to citizens of other States, while claiming free speech in Delaware and other Southern States. The treatment that Harris has received in Chester, New Castle and Wilmington from the Republicans is precisely the contrary of what the press of the Republican party has been demanding should be accorded in the South. But we do not find them offering protection to Harris. On the contrary they speak of this treatment of Harris in such a manner as to show they are pleased rather than displeased at it. If Harris had promised to deliver a Republican address to a mixed crowd of negroes and poor whites the Radical press would have been delighted. The hypocrisy of the Republicans is shown in this as it is in claiming the votes of the negroes as brothers on an equality and at the same time excluding the negroes from all their tickets and with a very few exceptions from all political offices that are worth having. They have sufficient majority in several of the Wards in this city to elect a Republican, but they have never put a "colored brother" on the ticket. Why is this? The Democrats of the South elect negroes to office. But the Radicals of Wilmington whose press always wars on the South for alleged illiberality toward the negroes, does not once propose to run negroes on the Republican ticket for office. Now, we make no complaint of this. But simply wish to show how inconsistent our Republicans are. They want others to do just what they will not do themselves. They would have other white people to send their children to schools to be taught with negroes, but they will not do it themselves.
john-h-harris-newcastle-1880-07-31.A20: Truly the love that our neighbors North of Mason and Dixon's line feel for their colored brethren is rapidly on the increase. John H. Harris, a colored Democratic speaker from Virginia, attempted to make a speech at Newcastle, Delaware, on the 31st ult., but was stoned by a Republican mob and forced to seek the protection of the Sheriff. Won't some of our Republican friends explain this matter?
john-h-harris-newcastle-1880-07-31.A22:
AN OMITTED DISPATCH.
A special dispatch to the New York Herald from Wilmington, Delaware, August 2d, reports this: "John H. Harris, a colored Democratic speaker from Virginia, attempted to make a speech at Newcastle, Saturday night, and was stoned and forced to seek the protection of the Sheriff."

The Republican manager who has charge of the press dispatches to the Pacific coast took very good care to omit the above from his daily send-off. But had it been a Republican colored speaker who was assaulted, a dispatch of many lines and adapted to "fire the Northern heart" by "another Southern Outrage," with "Intimidation of Voters" added, would have been quickly sent here.
